lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mahmudual Islam and Nihad Kabir, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan Addl, AG with Kaiseruddin Ahmed DAG, Mashuque Hossain Ahmed AAG, Saidur Rahman AAG and Md. Sirajul Hoque AAG ----- For the Respondent No.1
parties:
Bangladesh Retired Government Employees Welfare Association, represented by its President Kafiluddin Mahmood and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary to the Ministry of Finance, Finance Division, Government of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed, J.: In this writ petition the petitioner No. 1 which is an association for the welfare of retired government employees and the petitioner Nos. 2 and 3 who are retired government employees and also office-bearers of the above association have mainly claimed superannuation pension for all pensioners on the basis of calculation of their pension according to pay as on 1.6.85 of the respective posts which the pensioners held at the time of their retirement irrespective of their respective dates of retirement. In short, they claim pension to be calculated on the basis of "presumptive pay" or the existing pay as on 1.6.85 of the post from which they respectively retired. There was another petitioner, namely, the petitioner No. 4, who also happened to be a retired government employee but died during the pendency of this writ petition. 

 2. The case of the petitioners emerging from the writ petition and the affidavits-in-reply filed by them is, that the petitioner No. 1 is an association of retired government employees of Bangladesh known as the Bangladesh Retired Government Employees Welfare Association registered under the Voluntary Social Welfare Agency (Registration and Control) Ordinance, 1961. Apart from being government employees themselves the petitioner No. 2 happened to be the President of the said association and the petitioner No. 3 happened to be the Vice-President of the said association. 

 3. According to the averment in the writ petition, the petitioner No. 2 joined the erstwhile Civil Service of Pakistan on 16.10.1950., After liberation of Bangladesh he served the Government of Bangladesh and retired on 3.3.1983 from the post of Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh. The petitioner No. 2 was appointed to the erstwhile Police Service of Pakistan on 7.1.1952 and after liberation of Bangladesh he served the Government of Bangladesh and retired on 1.8.83 from the post of Secretary to the Ministry of Defence. It is emphasised that since British Rule in India the Government employees are being paid superannuation pension by the government and this pension to the retired employees is not a bounty paid by the State but is an essential term and condition of their service and is paid on consideration of the obligation of the State not to leave its employees who rendered service in the useful span of life to penury in their old age and disability and infirmity of their body and mind. According to the petitioners, apart from a statutory obligation of the State the superannuation pension is aimed at providing the retired government employees a life free from want, of decency and self-respect, and according to the standard equivalent to their pre-retirement level. Moreover, the pension paid to retired government employees is governed by Civil Service Regulations and various other Rules. It is also stated that initially the system of pension was introduced by the then government of India under British Rule in the year 1924 and, subsequently, the Rules relating to pension underwent various changes and the rates of pension were thereby modified. In short, prior to 1.7.66 the rate of pension was 50% of average pay of a government employee calculated on the basis of a certain table on completion of 25 years of service or more. With effect from 1.7.66 the rate of pension was revised under Notification No. F/IU-12/66/93 dated 2.9.66 and by this the rate of pension was fixed at 50% of average pay on completion of 25 years of service and 60% of average pay on completion of 30 years of service and the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 1000.00 per month. With effect from 1.7.74 by issuing Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21.1.74 the rate of pension was fixed at 60% of the last pay drawn on completion of 25 years of service. With effect from 1.7.77 the scale of pension was again revised by Notification No. MF(ID)-1-2/77/856 dated 20.12.77 whereby the maximum ceiling of pension was raised to Taka 1500.00 per month. With effect from 1.7.82 the rate of pension was again revised by issuing Notification No. MFP (FD) Regn-1/3P-22/82-147 dated 21.12.82 and MFP (FD) Regn-1/3P-22/82-117 dated 1.8.83 and by these notifications the rate of pension was fixed at 60% of the last pay on completion of 25 years of service and the minimum pension was fixed at Taka 100.00 per month and the maximum ceiling was raised to Taka 1800.00 per month. With effect from 1.6.85 the rate of pension was again revised and fixed at 70% of the last pay on completion of 25 years of service the maximum ceiling being fixed at Taka 4000.00 per month by issuing Notification No. MF (Regn- 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85. The last revision of the rate of pension took place with effect from 1.7.89 under Notification Nos. অম (বিধি)-১/৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/১০৬ dated 4.11.89 and অম (বিধি)-১/৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 whereby the rate of pension was raised to 80% of average pay on completion of 25 years of service and the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 5000.00 per month. On 1.7.91 by Notification No. অম/অবি (প্রবিধি)-৩ পি- ২৮/৮৫/৫০(১০০০) dated 4.12.91 the maximum ceiling was fixed at Taka 8200.00 per month. In this connection, it should be added that upto 1.7.74 i.e coming into force of the rate of pension vide Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21st January, 1974 calculation of average emoluments was specified and by this notification it was provided that the pension table should be made on the basis of emoluments which the government employee was receiving immediately before his retirement i.e. the last pay drawn by the government employee on the date of his retirement. The same principle has been followed in the latest Notification i.e. Memo No. ME (Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C to the writ petition which is impugned in this case. In addition to pension certain other benefits such as, commutation of pension and payment of lumpsum-amount in lieu thereof known as gratuity and of net payment of a lump-sum amount of 12 months salary last drawn by the government employees were also allowed to government employees on retirement. But these need not detain us here as these are not the subject-matter of controversy in this writ petition. It is next alleged by the petitioners that after liberation of Bangladesh there has been high inflation and the purchasing power of taka gradually eroded as a result of which the government of Bangladesh had to revise the pay scales of government employees in 1973, 1977 and 1985. As an example, it has been stated that in 1973 the pay of a Secretary to the Government was fixed at Taka 3000.00 per month and then ultimately the pay of the Secretary was raised to Taka 6000.00 per month in 1985. Similarly, the pay scale of the Deputy Secretary in 1973 was 850-1650 with certain special pay and this pay scale was revised and raised to Taka 1850-2075 and then ultimately to Taka 3700-4825 in the year 1985. As we have already observed, previous to 1974 the pension was to be calculated on the basis of emoluments drawn by a government employee during the 12 months preceding the date of his retirement. But with effect from 1.7.74 this was done away with and pension was to be calculated on the basis of the last pay drawn by each employee. According to the petitioners, by the pension rules brought into effect vide Memo No. MF(Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C, substantial difference in the pension benefit between the pensioners who had retired before 1.6.85 and those who retired on or after 1.6.85, was made. As an example, it has been stated that a Secretary to the Government who was drawing a salary of Taka 3000.00 per month retiring before 1.6.84 and between 1.6.84 and 31.5.85 is to draw a pension of Taka 900.00 per month, whereas a Secretary retiring on or after 1.6.85 was allowed to draw a net pension of Taka 2000.00 per month. Similarly, an employee retiring from the lowest scale of salary of Taka 225-315 was granted a pension of Taka 94.5 per month if retired prior to 1.6.84 and between 1.6.84 and 31.5.85, and Taka 258.00 per month if retired on or after 1.6.85. This obviously took place because of the revision of the scales of pay and enhancement of pay of all government employees before coming into force of the impugned pension rules on 1.6.85. The petitioners claim that all retired government employees receiving pension are pensioners forming a homogeneous class and, as such, payment of different scales of pension to the pensioners retiring from the service on the basis of the date of retirement is an irrational classification, violative of the equality clause enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution and, as such, cannot, be sustained and must be knocked down as unconstitutional. According to the petitioners, irrespective of the rise in pay scale of the government employees from time to time against which they have no grievance, all government employees retiring from a particular post being pensioners are entitled to receive pension on the basis of the existing ply of the said post. In short, they claim pension on "presumptive pay" irrespective of the dates of retirement. Although in this writ petition, ultimately the petitioners have mainly claimed computation of pension of all pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 on the basis of the pay of the post existing on that date or equivalent post if that post ceases to exist i.e. on "presumptive pay" these is another aspect in this case i.e. the constitutionality of the pension table introduced by Notification No. MF(Regn-1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C whereby the rate of pension was raised to 70% of the emoluments and also Notification No. অম (বিধি-১) ৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/১০৬ dated 4.11.89 whereby the table was again revised and the rate of pension was raised to 80% of the emoluments or last pay drawn on completion of 25 years' service. Along with this the rate of pension was also raised according to the length of service of each employee the minimum qualifying service being 10 years and the maximum being 25 years. According to the petitioners, the payment of different rates of pension to the pensioners retiring from the cadre post prior to 1.6.85 from those retiring from the same post on or after 1.6.85 has been absolutely arbitrary being contrary to the principle of classification and, therefore, violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. 

 4. In order to seek remedy against such unjust classification resulting in discrimination against the pensioners who had retired before 1.6.1985, the petitioners moved several authorities including the Financial Adviser-in-charge of the Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh, and ultimately the President of Bangladesh, but to no effect. On the other hand, in response to their representation to the President of Bangladesh they were informed by letter No. ৩(৬১)- গোপ/৮৭-৭৩০ dated 21.11.87 that the pensioners retiring before 1.6.85 were not entitled to equalisation of their pension with the pensioners retiring on or after 1.6.85 and this letter is at Annexure-H to the writ petition. 

 6. The respondent No. 1, Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance Division, Government of Bangladesh, entered appearance and contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. The contesting respondent challenges the allegation of the petitioners made in paragraph 7 of the writ petition to the effect that pension is not a bounty paid by the State, but is an essential term and condition of service of a government employee and that the object of pension is to provide a life to a pensioner free from want and with decency equivalent to the standard enjoyed by him while he was on service. It is then contended by the contesting respondent that the State had no legal or contractual obligation to undertake the entire responsibility of bearing the expenses of maintaining the standard of living of a pensioner equal to the standard of living he enjoyed during pre-retirement life. It is, however, contended that the government has every intention and wish to see that an employee retiring from service lives a decent standard of life and with this end in view, the government provides pensioners benefits within its limited financial resources. The contesting respondent also contends that since the pensioners are no longer in service they cannot claim enhancement of their pension once fixed according to rule by enforcing any legal right and the government has also no legal obligation to revise the pension of the pensioners with the revision of pay-scales of the government employee in service. In spite of this legal position, along with the revision of the rate of pension of the employees who retired or will retire on or after 1.6.85 the pensioners who had retired prior to 1.6.85 were also allowed substantial benefits in the form of dearness allowances. It is also contended that classification of pensioners on the basis of the date of effect of the enhanced rate of pension is a valid and rational classification and, as such, cannot be conceived to be violative of Article 27 of the Constitution. It is also contended that every legislative enactment and every governmental action, particularly, where the legislative enactment or the governmental action is a financial measure, a specific date has to be fixed for giving effect to such legislative enactment or governmental action and fixing such date, even it if results in classification in securing benefit to a class or group of people while securing no such benefit to another class or group of people, cannot be deemed to be violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. It has further been contended that impugned notification being Notification No. MF(Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 being applicable to government servants who were in employment on 1.6.85 and retired on or after 1.6.85 cannot be made applicable to those who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and has ceased to become government employees, because, the government employees who had retired prior to 1.6.85 form a class distinct from the government employees who were in service on 1.6.85 and retired thereafter. As such, according to the contesting respondent, the government employees who retired from service prior to 1.6.85 cannot legally claim revision of their rates of pension once fixed according to rules. They are not, therefore, entitled to pension to be determined according to or on the basis of presumptive revised pay as admissible to government employees from 1.6.85. This writ petition must, therefore, be dismissed. 

 8. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, has submitted that all pensioners, irrespective of their respective dates of retirement, form a single homogeneous class and for the purpose of allowing pension- benefits this single homogeneous class cannot be sub-divided into various classes with reference to the respective dates of their retirement. It has been urged by him that the impugned notification revising the pension rules and raising the rate of pension has classified the pensioners into those who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and those who retired on or after 1.6.85 and thereby made discrimination between the pensioners as a class as to the amount of pension granted to them. According to Mr. Ahmed, the selection of a particular date for making the classification has been absolutely arbitrary and has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the revised rule of pension emerging from the impugned notification being Notification No. MF (Regn-1) 3P-28/86/60 dated 10.8.85. In this connection, Mr. Ahmed has also challenged the notification issued under Memo No. MF (IC)-11-14/47 dated 21.1.1974 whereby it was decided to grant pension "on the basis of emoluments which the government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement". According to Mr. Ahmed, the calculation of pension on the basis of emoluments immediately before retirement has the effect of making discrimination in the rate of pension when the pay-scales of the government employees are revised and enhanced, and as such, according to him, all pensioners, irrespective of their dates of retirement, are entitled to receive pension calculated on the basis of the pay of the post or presumptive pay whenever pay scale is revised upwards. Mr. Ahmed wants to say that the manner of calculating pension on the basis of last pay drawn is illogical and irrational having no nexus with the object of granting pension i.e. to provide equal relief to all pensioners retiring from the same post. According to him, as soon as the pay scale of the post of a pensioner is revised and enhanced the rule of calculating pension according to the last pay drawn by him becomes violative of Article 27 of the Constitution, and as such, there should be an upward revision of his pension calculated on the basis of the existing pay of the post after revision of pay. In order to further elaborate, Mr. Ahmed has submitted that the object of the impugned notification whereby the rate of pensions was revised and enhanced being to secure all pensioners against penury, the object is not achieved in respect of a class of pensioners i.e. those who had retired prior to 1.6.85, as they were left out of this benefit and the benefit is confined to another class of pensioners i.e. those who retired on or after 1.6.85. By classifying them with reference to their respective dates of retirement the object of the enhanced rate of pension is denied to one class of pensioners, and as such, the object is not achieved. Consequently, the provisions contained in the legislative enactment or governmental action denying the benefit of enhanced pension to a class of pensioners become at once arbitrary and, therefore, violative of Article 27 of the Constitution, and, Mr. Ahmed has argued, a pensioner who was in the same post or equal post is entitled to get his pension equalised with the pension of the pensioner retiring from the same post after enhancement of the pay-scale of the post. Mr. Ahmed has further submitted that the need for pension for all pensioners being the same i.e. to allow them to live a modestly decent life free from penury, all1fpensioners irrespective of their dates of retirement are entitled to equal protection of law as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution, and as such, any legislative enactment or governmental action that deprives them of such entitlement being violative of Article 27 cannot be sustained. 

 13. After arguing the above preliminary points the learned Additional Attorney-General has contended that pension of government employees is regulated by Rule 4 of the Civil Service Regulations and according to this Rule, pension to a government servant is regulated and payable by the Rules in force at the time when the officer resigns or retires or is discharged from the service of Government. He has also referred to Rule 509 of the Civil Service Regulations which provides that pension is to be calculated upon the net pay i.e. the pay actually received by the officer. He has also referred to the meaning of "pay" as defined in Rule 486 of the Civil Service Regulations and also to the definition of "pay" as in Rule 5(40) of the Bangladesh Service Rules. He also depended on the pension rules announced by Notification No. MF(IC)-II-14/74 dated 21.1.74 wherein it has been provided that pension shall be calculated according to the emoluments which the government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement and has then argued that the petitioners and, so to say, all pensioners are bound by these rules, and as such, they cannot claim pension in contravention of these rules and also cannot claim calculation of pension on the basis of enhanced emoluments resulting from introduction of the revised pay scale as their emoluments were not the same immediately before their retirement. The learned Additional Attorney- General has also quoted the principles of granting pension, particularly from the American Jurisprudence, and has contended that in view of the above principles of law the petitioner or, so to say, the pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 cannot claim pension on the basis of their presumptive pay. 

 14. The next line of argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General has been that all financial measures must have a date of coming into effect and in this connection, he has referred to AIR 1974 (SC) 2349 and AIR 1980 (SC) 272 and has argued that as all financial acts of the government and all financial enactments must contain the date on which such act or enactment should come into effect and for the fact that such effective date has deprived certain class of persons of the benefit of the financial measure, such measure cannot be called in question by terming such measure as violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. 

 18. The locus standi of the petitioner No. 1 which is an association of retired government employees named Bangladesh Retired Government Employees Welfare Association has been called in question on the ground that such an association cannot be deemed to be a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution. The learned Additional Attorney-General has relied upon a decision of this Court reported in 43 DLR 424. In reply, Mr. Ahmed has drawn our attention to the observations of the Supreme Court of India in DS Nakara and others Vs. Union of India, AIR 1983 (SC) 130. In this case, the locus standi of the petitioner No. 3 in the writ petition before the said Court was seriously challenged on the ground that the petitioner No. 3 which was a Society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1960 and a non-political, non-profit, voluntary organisation could not have any standing to challenge the pension rules of government employees as these rules did not affect the said Society. Its members consisted of public-spirited citizens who took up the cause of ventilating legitimate public problems and it instituted the writ petition on behalf of the pensioners who were individually unable to undertake the arduous journey of fighting a litigation in a court of Jaw. It was held in this case by the Supreme Court of India as follows: 

 20. Let us now refer to the case of the Pakistan Jurisdiction on which the learned Additional Attorney-General has himself placed reliance. This case is IA Sharwani and others Vs. Government of Pakistan and others decided by the Pakistan Supreme Court and reported in 1991 SCMR 1041. In that case, four writ petitions were filed, two of which were by two retired civil servants one of whom was ultimately elevaied as a judge of a High Court, and one being an association of GHQ retired civilian officers and the other being an association for the welfare of retired persons and in all the four writ petitions the dispute was relating to the pension benefit granted to government pensioners. The locus standi of the two associations was seriously questioned and it was argued for the government that these associations having no interest in the matter had no locus standi and were not, therefore, competent to file these writ petitions. After considering several cases decided by the Pakistan Supreme Court and the Indian Supreme Court including DS Nakara's case the SP Gupta's case, it was held as follows: 

 21. Clause (3) of Article 183 of the Constitution of Pakistan vests the Supreme Court of Pakistan with very wide powers to pass any order in the nature of an order under Article 199 of that Constitution on any question which it considers to be of public importance with reference to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights enshrined in Chapter I of Part II of that Constitution. Although such wide powers are not as .specifically vested in the High Court Division by our Constitution as in the Supreme Court of Pakistan by the Pakistan Constitution, the learned Additional Attorney-General has not disputed that the petitioner No.1 is an association for looking after the welfare of the retired government employees and the question of pension of the retired government employee is a question in which the common interests of all retired government employees arc involved and, as such, to our view, it is an absurd proposition to suggest each individual pensioner to come forward and file a separate writ petition vindicating a common right. There is no. doubt that since the petitioner No. 1 looks after the common interests of all retired government employees it is entitled to ventilate this interest before this Court in the form of public interest litigation. Apart from this there in another aspect involved in the question of locus standi of the petitioner No. 1. In this connection, we have to fall back on clause (1) of Article 102 of the Constitution which runs as follows: 

 There is no dispute that the Bangladesh Retired Government Servants Welfare Association is an association registered under the Voluntary Social Welfare Agencies (Registration and Control) Ordinance, 1961 (Ordinance No. XLVI of 1961). It, therefore, appears that its activities are authorised by the above Ordinance and, as such, this association can be deemed to be a body within the meaning of the definition of "statutory public authority" as defined in Article 152 of the Constitution. So, by operation of Clause (5) of Article 102 of the Constitution this association is a "person" within the meaning of Clause (1) and Clause (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution. Since this association has an interest in ventilating the common grievance of all its members who are retired government employees, to our view, this association is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Clause (1) and Clause (2) of Article 102 of the Constitution. It is, therefore, entitled to maintain this writ petition. 

 22. We have noticed the decision reported in 43 DLR 424. In this case, the Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad which was an association of newspaper-owners as petitioner challenged the decision of the Wage Board and it was held by this Court that the owners and the employees of newspapers who were affected by the award could challenge it and the Bangladesh Sangbadpatra Parishad had no locus standi to challenge the award of the Wage Board. The facts of that case do not fit in with the facts of the present case and, as such, the principle set out in the said case cannot be applied to this case. It is true that in a number of cases, such as Dada Match Workers Union (Bargaining Agent) Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 29 DLR 188; Tariq Transport Company, Lahore Vs. The Sargodha Bhera Bus Service, reported in 11 DLR (SC) 140; Khulna Shipyard Employees Union Vs. General Manager, Khulna Shipyard and others, reported in 30 DLR 368 and Zamiruddin Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 34 DLR 34, it has been consistently held that a "person aggrieved" means a person whose personal interest is affected by a legislative enactment or a governmental action and generally an association cannot have locus standi to vindicate the rights of persons who themselves do not approach the court and, in this way, the words "person aggrieved" have been interpreted to decide the locus standi of the petitioners in those cases. 

 (b) the acquisition, administration management and disposal of any property vested in or managed by the Government by or under any law, including 'the operation and management of, and service in any nationalised enterprise or statutory public authority; 

 29. There is no doubt that in this writ petition the petitioners seek to enforce fundamental right enshirned in Article 27 of the Constitution and by enforcing this fundamental right the petitioners challenge the vires of the pension rules as embodied in Memo No. MF(Regn-1)3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C to the writ petition and also the pension rules as embodied in Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21.1.74 as at Annexure- B to the writ petition. It is undisputed .that these two notifications are law within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution. The Administrative Tribunal, in exercise of its power under Clause (1) of Article 117 of the Constitution, cannot knock down a law on the ground of its unconstitutionality, and as such, it appears, that the Administrative Tribunal is not competent to entertain this case in which the petitioners have prayed for knocking down a certain provision of law contained in Annexure- B and Annexure-C of the writ petition. Since the Administrative Tribunal does not have any jurisdiction to knockdown the aforesaid provisions of law we find that it has no jurisdiction to decide this matter and as such, Clause (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution ousting the jurisdiction of this Court is not attracted, In this connection, Mujibur Rahman Vs. Government of Bangladesh decided by the learned Appellate Division of "this Court and reported in 44 DLR (AD) 11 may be relied upon. In this case, it was held, 

 The undersigned is directed to say that the Government of Bangladesh has had under consideration the revision of Pension Table annexed to the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan, Finance Department (Implementation Unij) memorandum No. F/lU-12/66/93, dated the 2nd September, 1966 reproduced at page 305 of BSR, Part I (1970 edition) so as to relax the maximum limit of Pension. The question of general liberalisation of pension has been examined in the light of the orders regarding retiring Government servants on completion of 25 years of qualifying service. The President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has been pleased to revise the new pension table annexed to the above quoted memo dated the 2nd September, 1966 as shown in Annexure A to this memorandum. The calculation of pension, according to the scale shown in column 2 of the Pension Table, should be made on the basis of emoluments which the Government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement and if he proceeds on LPR, on the basis of emoluments, which he was receiving immediately before proceeding on LPR. The term "emoluments" for determining pension shall mean "emoluments" as defined in paragraph 7(5) of the above quoted memorandum, dated the 2nd September, 1966. If at the time of retirement or of proceeding on LPR, the pay of a Government servant was subject to any cut his "presumptive" pay at the time which he would receive had the cut not been imposed, but subject to the maximum limit of pay of his post as may have' been ordered by the Government and in force at the time of retirement should be taken as included in his "emoluments" for the purpose of calculations of pension…………………." 

 The other portions of the notification are not material as the petitioners have challenged the provision in this notification regarding, "the calculation of pension…………..on the basis of emoluments which the Government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement and if he proceeds on LPR, on the: basis of emoluments which he, was receiving immediately before proceeding on LPR………………………" 

 It should be made clear that when this notification was issued and this provision was included there was no grievance of any pensioner and the grievance actually originated after the introduction of the revised pay scale as a result of which the pay of government servants was revised as a consequence of which those who hanrctired before introduction of the revised pay scale had been on receipt of emoluments which was less than the emoluments of those who retired after the introduction of the revised pay scale. Naturally, pensioners retiring from the same post would get lower amount as pension if retired before introduction of the revised pay scale than the amount of pension of those who retired or may retire after the introduction of the revised pay scale, because, according to the notification, the calculation of pension has to be made on the basis of emoluments which the government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement. According to this notification the term "emoluments" means emoluments as defined "in Para 7(5) of the Notification No. F/IU-12/66/93, dated the 2nd September, 1966 reproduced at page 305 of BSR, Part I (1970 edition). According to it, the terms emoluments in Para 7(5) of the above notification as reproduced at page 305 of BSR Part 1(1970) is defined as follows: 

 "The term "Emoluments", shall mean the emoluments which the Government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement and shall include: 

 So, according to the above definition, emoluments mean the pay including special pay, technical pay, personal pay, etc. last drawn by a government employee immediately before his retirement. After revision of the pay scale, naturally the last pay of the government employee retiring from a post before such revision would be lower than the pay of a government employee retiring from the same post after introduction of the revised pay scale, .and as such, in view of the effect of Notification No. MF(lC)-11-14/74 dated 21.1.74, consequent upon calculation of pension on the basis of last pay drawn the pension of the government employee retiring before introduction of the revised pay scale would be lower than the pension of the government employee retiring after introduction of the revised pay scale although both the government employees might have retired from the same post and that is precisely what has happened in case of the petitioners after coming into force of Notification No. MF (Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85. It should also be noted that the provision to calculate pension on the basis of emoluments which the government servant was receiving immediacy before retirement was not introduced by this notification as at Annexure-C, but was introduced by the previous Notification No. MF(IC)-11-14/74 dated 21.1.74 as at Annexure-B. In view of the provision to calculate pension according to the emoluments received by a government employee immediately before his retirement in accordance with the provision of this notification dated 21.1.74, Annexure-B, the difference in pension after introduction of the later notification i.e. Notification No. MF(Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 as at Annexure-C took place and, as such, the petitioners what to say that since the effect of the notification as at Annexure-B has resulted in granting different rates of pension to the government employees retiring from the same post, the provision regarding calculation of pension on the basis of emoluments which the government employee was receiving immediately before his retirement is violative of the equality clause as defined in Article 27 of the Constitution and is, therefore, liable to be knocked down. 

 33. The second attack is confined to the notifications under Memo Nos. MF(Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 and No. ম/বিধি-১/তপি-২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 whereby the rate of pension was increased twice by revising the table of pension, on the ground that this revision was given effect to from 1.6.85 and 1.7.89 respectively thereby classifying the pensioners arbitrarily into two classes, that is, those who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and those who retired subsequent to 1.6.85 and also between those who had retired prior to 1.7.89 and those who retired subsequent to 1.7.89. According to the petitioner, this classification between pensioners for granting the benefit of the enhanced rate of pension under these notifications on the basis of the date of retirement of a government employee has been absolutely arbitrary having no nexus with the object of the enhancement made under the aforesaid two notifications and, as such, are violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and the provision relating to fixing of dates for giving effect to these notifications must be knocked down as unconstitutional. 

 "The decisions clearly lay down that though Article 14 forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purpose of legislation. In order, however, to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled, viz., (i) that the classification must be found on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from those that are left out of the group; and (ii) that differentia must have a rational relation to the objects sought "to be achieved by the statute in question. (See Ram Krishna DalmiaVs. SR Tendolkar, 1959 SCR 279 at pa 296: (AIR 1958 SC at p. 547). 

 Along with the above interpretation of the equality clause let us refer to IA Sharwani and others Vs. Government of Pakistan, reported in 1991 SCMR (Supreme Court Monthly Review) 1041 decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan only recently.. After citing several decisions of the Indian Supreme Court including DS Nakara and others Vs. Union of India and various decisions of the Pakistan Supreme Court it was held as follows: 

 38. It, therefore, appears that the equality clause does not necessarily mean that every law or governmental action must always have similar application to all persons irrespective of differences of circumstances and the principle does not take away from the legislature or the government the power of classifying persons for the purpose of the applicability of a law or governmental action provided the classification meets the twin tests of rationality and nexus with the object of legislation or governmental action. The plain meaning of this clause is that for classification two conditions must be fulfilled and the first of these conditions is that the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia that distinguished the persons who are grouped together from others who are left out of the group and, secondly, that the differentia must have a rational relation or nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the legislative enactment or the governmental action in question. 

 39. We have now to consider whether the impugned notifications meet the above twin tests and for this purpose we will first of all take up the provision relating to the calculation of pension of retired government employees on the basis of the last emoluments drawn by them. 

 41. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned counsel, has argued that the only object of granting pension to retired government employees is to sustain them in their old age when their physical and mental capabilities wane, in exchange for the service rendered by them in the prime of their life. According to him, since the object of granting pension is to sustain the pensioners, the rate of pension must be enhanced with the rise in costs of living. 

 42. The learned Additional Attorney-General has contended that to demand rise in the rate of pension would mean providing extra benefits to those who are no longer in the employment of the government, and as such, to make extra payment to them from the public exchequer will be unconstitutional. In support of his contention he has relied on the following observations in the American Jurisprudence: 

 "Statutes that purport to grant pensions to persons already retired from public employment at the time of the enactment are generally considered to be unconstitutional as amounting to gratuities for a private purpose, or as within prohibition against the giving of extra compensation to a public officer or .employee after the services have been rendered or the like. The same general rule applies to an attempt to provide pension benefits to survivors of a pensioner where there was no provision for such benefits prior to the pensioner's retirement. The principle that pension systems are only valid in regard to individuals who at the time of the enactment are officers or employees of the governmental entity, has been extended so far as to deny the power of a municipality to pay a pension which is based even in part upon services rendered prior to the enactment of the statute establishing the system, though most courts passing on this point have held to the contrary." (60A Am Jur 2nd, para 1607, page 940-941). Again, "Some state and local pension systems provide that a pensioner's benefits may be adjusted according to a cost of living formula. Where the state constitution forbids the payment of extra compensation to employees who are already retired, however, pension payments under a statute authorising cost of living adjustments to policemen who retired prior to effective date of the statute are unconstitutional. Further, a provision that pensions should rise as the cost of living rises is also unconstitutional where it fails to state to whom authority is granted to make a determination of whether the cost of living has gone up, and where there are no standards set by which such a determination can be made. Where legislation provides for a cost of living adjustment for pension benefits, the legislature may not put a cap on the level of the adjustment in regard to employees whose rights are already vested if there was no cap previously imposed, at least where no comparable new advantage is provided. A cost of living increase in a retirement allowance, once granted by a town, becomes vested in the year when granted in the absence of a legislative intent to condition such an increase." (60A Am Jur. 2d., para 1706, page 1025-1026). 

 43. The learned Additional Attorney-General has not, however, disputed that in our country pension as a statutory right of a government employee is governed by statutory rules and one of the main objects of superannuation pension is to provide sustenance to the retired government employees. This object of granting pension is universally accepted and indisputable. 

 44. We have now to find out, whether apart from securing this object of providing sustenance to the retired government employees this notification as at Annexure-B had any other object and whether the said object has any nexus with the inevitable classification that has resulted from this notification after upward revision of the pay scale of the government employees. A close perusal of the offending portion, that is, the portion which runs as follows: 

 "The calculation of pension according to the scale shown in column 2 of the Pension Table should be made on the basis of emoluments which the Government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement and if he proceeds on LPR, on the basis of emoluments which he was receiving immediately before proceeding on LPR," 

 shows that apart from granting sustenance to retired government employees the other object of this notification was to calculate pension for providing such sustenance on the basis of the last pay drawn by a government employee. The second object of this notification was, therefore, to pay pension after calculating pension on the basis of emoluments which the government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement. This object inevitably created different classes of pensioners, such as, the pensioner who retired on the last emoluments of Taka 100.00 and the petitioner who retired on the last emoluments of Taka 1000.00. Since it appears to us that the object of this notification was to sustain the retirees by paying pension according to the last emoluments drawn by them the classification made by it between pensioners according to the amount of last emoluments drawn by them had nexus with this second object in this notification. As such, the twin tests of classification, that is, grouping together of pensioners on the basis of the last pay drawn by them has a rational basis and this grouping together is related to the object sought to be secured by the offending portion of this notification, that is, the object of granting pension to a government employee on the basis of emoluments which the government employee was receiving immediately before his retirement. It, therefore, appears to us that this offending portion of the notification as at Annexure-B meets the twin tests of classification, and as such, it cannot be said to be violative of Article 27 of the Constitution for causing classification among pensioners on the basis of the last emoluments drawn by them. 

 45. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, has not contended that this Principle of calculating pension on the basis of the last pay drawn by the government employees had been irrational or arbitrary, at least when the notification was issued on 21st January, 1974. Mr. Ahmed also argues that persons retiring from different posts are differently circumstance for the purpose of payment of pension and, as such, classification of persons retiring from different posts for fixing the rate of their pension is not irrational and does not violate the equality clause. If persons retiring from different posts are not equally circumstanced, then persons retiring on different salaries are not also equally circumstanced. This principle of calculating pension on the basis of the last pay drawn which the government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement, therefore, appears to us to be absolutely a rational principle and based on sound reasoning, because, different scales of pay for different posts are inevitable-To conceive that for the purpose of calculating pension a pensioner retiring from a post prior to revision of the pay of the said post belongs to the same class as the pensioner retiring from that post after revision of the pay of the post is to conceive that the former's pay on retirement was the same as the revised pay or that he was in service on the date of revision of the pay scale, both of which are fiction. So, for the purpose of calculation of pension the classification of pensioners on the basis of the last pay drawn is a real and rational classification. Mr. Ahmed has attacked this provision being discriminatory due to its effect after the upward revision of the pay scale of government employees. It is true that as an effect of this provision a pensioner retiring from a post would get an amount as pension lower than a pensioner who retires from the same post after the pay scale of the said post is revised upward. But, this effect cannot attract the mischief of Article 27 of the Constitution if once the principle of calculation of pension on the basis of emoluments a government servant was receiving immediately before his retirement was found not to be repugnant to Article 27 of the Constitution. 

 46. We therefore, find that the principle set out in the notification as at Annexure-B of calculating pension on the basis of emoluments which a government employee was receiving immediately before his retirement nor its effect on the rate of pension of the retirees after upward revision of the "scale of pay of the post which the retiree was holding before his retirement, is violative of the equality clause as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution.

 50. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has argued that the object of the enhancement of the rate of pension by these two notifications was obvious and that was to render sustenance to the retired government servants in view of rising costs of living and the diminishing value of currency on account of uncontrollable inflation. 

 51. The learned Additional Attorney-General has not seriously disputed the proposition that the enhancement of the rate of pension was aimed at providing sustenance to the retired government employees. 

 We find that this classification on the basis of the date of retirement has hardly any nexus with the object sought to be achieved by these two notifications, that is, making provision for sustenance of the retired government employees in the face of the rising cost of living. 

 As such, we find that this classification, on the basis of the date of retirement, between those pensioners who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and those who retired subsequent to 1.6.85 for the purpose of applicability of these two notifications has been arbitrary and, therefore, repugnant to the very concept of equality and equal protection of law as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. This offending portion whereby the government employees who had retired prior to 1.6.85 were denied the benefit of the enhanced rate of pension as provided in these two notifications must, accordingly, be deemed to be unconstitutional as violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and knocked down. 

 53. We are not unaware that the government granted certain dearness allowances to the pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 and the learned Additional Attorney-General placed before us the notifications whereby dearness allowances were granted to them. These are Notification No. MF(Regn I-I) 3P-28/82/73 dated 21.7.86 and Notification No. অম/(অবি) প্রবি-২/মন্ডা-২/৮৭/১২৪ dated 27.7.1987. We have heard the learned Additional Attorney-General to say that in the light of granting dearness allowance the pensioners are not entitled to any further increase in pension. We have already found that the exclusion of the pensioners from the benefits of Notification Nos. MR(Regn-1)-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 have been violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and, as such, the offending portion is liable to be knocked down as a result of which the pensioners will be legally entitled to the benefits of these two notifications. By allowing the benefits of dearness allowance the pensioners cannot, therefore be deprived of their legal right to get the benefits of these notifications. 

 55. The learned Additional Attorney-General has also submitted that to direct the government to calculate pension of the pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 according to Notification No. MF(Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 and Notification No. অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 will tantamount to legislation in the way of amending those notifications and this the Court cannot undertake. We are not legislating by declaring the offending portion of the notifications as unconstitutional. We are merely interpreting a measure in the light of the Constitution and cutting down its offending portion being unconstitutional while retaining the rest of it and that is what is precisely the constitutional duty cast upon this Court by Article 102 

 56. The respondents must, accordingly, be directed to calculate the pension of all pensioners according to the rate as at the Annexures to these two notifications irrespective of their dates of retirement. It must also be remembered that the retired government employees would also be entitled to the benefit of dearness allowance allowed to them from time to time. 

 57. Mr. Ahmed has high-lighted the apparent inequity of the effect of calculating pension on the basis of the last emoluments drawn by the government employees and as an example he has cited the case of a Secretary retiring before 1.6.85 and getting a net pension of Taka 900.00 per month and a Secretary retiring on or after l. 7.91 getting a net pension of Taka 4000.00 per month. Similarly, he cited the case of an employee in the lowest scale of pay who retired before 1.6.85 and getting a pension of Taka 94.5 per month and the employee retiring from the same post on or after 1.7.91 getting a net pension of Taka 612.00 per month. We have no doubt that the effect of calculating pension on the basis of the last emoluments drawn has resulted in great inequity between government employees retiring from the same post as a result of upward revision of pay in view of the rising costs of living and depreciation of the value of currency. But, a legislative enactment or a governmental action cannot be knocked down as unconstitutional even if it results in inequity, is even shocking to the conscience and apparently unjust, unless such enactment or such action is violative of any provision of the Constitution in the former and the Constitution or any other law in the latter. As such, this inequity and unconscionable effect cannot be rectified by this Court by applying Article 27 of the Constitution. Probably, it is for the government to remove such inequity by implementing one of the Fundamental Principles of State Policy enshrined in Part II of the Constitution, particularly, Article 15 (d) of the Constitution, So far as the case of the pensioners is concerned.
